issuing_office: Human Foods Program
subject: CGMP/Manufacturing, Packaging, Labeling, or Holding Operations for Dietary Supplements/Adulterated
text: Dear Mr. Betz: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) conducted an inspection of your facility located at 10601 Decatur Rd Ste 2, Philadelphia, PA 19154 from May 12 through June 8, 2026. Based on inspectional findings and review of the product labels collected during the inspection, we have identified significant violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (the Act) and applicable regulations. You can find the Act and FDA regulations through links on FDA's home page at www.fda.gov. At the conclusion of the inspection on June 8, 2026, our investigator provided you with a Form FDA 483, Inspectional Observations (FDA 483). We have not received a response to Form FDA 483 as of the date on this letter. Adulterated Dietary Supplements The inspection of your facility from May 12 through June 8, 2026, identified serious violations of the FDA’s regulations for Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) in Manufacturing, Packaging, Labeling, or Holding Operations for Dietary Supplements, under Title 21, Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), Part 111 (21 CFR Part 111). These violations cause the Ashwagandha Root, Mexican Sarsaparilla Root, and Black Walnut Hulls dietary supplement products manufactured at your facility to be adulterated within the meaning of section 402(g)(1) of the Act [21 U.S.C. 342(g)(1)] because they have been prepared, packed, or held under conditions that do not meet CGMP requirements for dietary supplements. Your significant violations of the CGMP requirements are as follows: 1. You failed to establish, for each component that you use in the manufacture of a dietary supplement, identity specifications and component specifications regarding limits on those types of contamination that may adulterate or may lead to adulteration of the finished batch of dietary supplement to ensure the quality of the dietary supplement, as required by 21 CFR 111.70(b)(1) and (b)(3). Specifically: You failed to establish identity specifications for the component Mexican Sarsaparilla Root (used in the production of your dietary supplement product Mexican Sarsaparilla Root); and the component Black Walnut Hulls, (used in the production of your dietary supplement Black Walnut Hulls), as required by 21 CFR 111.70(b)(1). Specifically, your firm's "Receiving and Component Analysis" document for the component Mexican Sarsaparilla Root in powder form, botanical name of Smilax officinalis, under "Gross Organoleptic Analysis” states that you confirm the identity by evaluating appearance (whole/cut/powder), color (light brown, reddish brown to pale brown), taste (mucilaginous, bitter, weak), and aroma (sweet, spicy). However, because other sarsaparilla-producing Smilax species share the same or similar organoleptic characteristics, including appearance, color, taste, and aroma, analysis of these organoleptic factors does not provide unique information specific to Smilax officinalis and therefore cannot, by itself, confirm the species-level identity of Smilax officinalis. Your firm's "Receiving and Component Analysis" document for the component Black Walnut Hulls in powder form, botanical name Juglans nigra, under “Gross Organoleptic Analysis” states that you confirm the identity by evaluating the appearance (whole/cut/powder), color (dark brown), taste (bitter, woody), and aroma (woody). However, because other botanical materials, including other Juglans species, share the same or similar organoleptic characteristics, including appearance, color, taste, and aroma, analysis of these organoleptic factors does not provide unique information specific to Juglans nigra. Therefore, these organoleptic characteristics alone are not sufficiently specific to confirm the species-level identity of your powdered Black Walnut Hulls component, botanical name Juglans nigra. You also include a link under identity verification process to a CoA sheet for Black Walnut Hull Powder Herb (b)(4), which includes additional organoleptic characteristics (aroma – earthy, slightly bitter, nutty). The additional attributes increase the descriptive detail of the component but do not provide sufficiently specific characteristics to distinguish and verify its botanical identity. You failed to establish limits on those types of contamination that may adulterate or that may lead to adulteration of the finished batch of the dietary supplement, as required by 21 CFR 111.70(b)(3). Specifically, you have not established limits on contaminants such as microbes and heavy metals that may be present in your dietary ingredients Ashwagandha Root, Mexican Sarsaparilla Root, and Black Walnut Hulls. In addition to establishing the required specifications, your firm must demonstrate whether such specifications are met, in accordance with 21 CFR 111.73 and 111.75. 2. You failed to establish product specifications for the identity, purity, strength, and composition of the finished batch of the dietary supplement, and for limits on those types of contamination that may adulterate, or that may lead to adulteration of, the finished batch of the dietary supplement to ensure the quality of the dietary supplement, as required by 21 CFR 111.70(e). Specifically, you have not established finished product specifications including identity, purity, strength, and composition, and limits on contamination for your finished dietary supplements Ashwagandha Root, Mexican Sarsaparilla Root, and Black Walnut Hulls. The established specification listed on each BPR is the weight of material per capsule in milligrams. Weight of material per capsule is not a specification to determine the identity, purity, strength, composition, and limits of contamination for these finished dietary supplement products. In addition to establishing the required finished product specifications, your firm must demonstrate whether the established specifications are met, in accordance with 21 CFR 111.73 and 111.75. 3. You failed to conduct all manufacturing operations in accordance with adequate sanitation principles, as required by 21 CFR 111.360. Specifically: During the walkthrough of the processing rooms, our investigator observed debris from previous production runs on food-contact surfaces of your (b)(4) encapsulator, including in the filled capsule collection/ejection chute. Powder debris was observed on the floor, walls, and ceilings of the encapsulator room and other manufacturing rooms. Powder residue was observed in the same processing room following pre-operational cleaning and sanitation conducted by your production employee, and prior to the initiation of production of your dietary supplement Mexican Sarsaparilla Root, Lot (b)(4). Your inadequate sanitation procedures risk contaminating your products. Our investigator observed residual dietary ingredient powder remaining after each encapsulation cycle which was being collected in a (b)(4) container for reuse in subsequent capsule production using a worn brush and other tools. The manufacturing employee stated that these tools were reused across production runs and cleaned between uses by spraying (b)(4) and wiping with a (b)(4). Collecting and reclaiming spilled or residual powder using worn, improperly sanitized tools, and introducing it back into production, is an unsanitary manufacturing practice that creates a significant risk of introducing foreign physical materials and microbial contamination into your finished dietary supplements. The sanitizing agent used to clean the food contact surfaces of your (b)(4) encapsulator was identified as “(b)(4). The product labeling identified it solely as a “(b)(4)” intended for external use on (b)(4). You were unable to provide evidence demonstrating that this agent was safe and suitable for use on food-contact surfaces in a dietary supplement manufacturing environment. The only employee hand-sink located outside of the individual manufacturing rooms was posted with an "Out of Order" sign at the time of inspection and during active production of dietary supplements. Multiple opened bulk bags of dietary supplement ingredients in the warehouse were observed resealed with tape, with some bags exhibiting loose or failing tape closures with dust debris on the exterior surfaces. This letter is not intended to be an all-inclusive statement of violations that may exist in connection with your products. You are responsible for investigating and determining the causes of any violations and for preventing their recurrence or the occurrence of other violations. It is your responsibility to ensure that your firm complies with all requirements of federal law, including FDA regulations. This letter notifies you of our concerns and provides you with an opportunity to address them. Failure to adequately address this matter may result in legal action including, without limitation, seizure and injunction. We also have the following comment: Section 201(qq)) of the Act [21 U.S.C. 321(qq)] defines milk, egg, fish, Crustacean shellfish, sesame, tree nuts, wheat, peanuts, and soybeans, as well as any food ingredient that contains protein derived from one of these foods, with the exception of highly refined oils, as "major food allergens." We note that your Black Walnut Hulls dietary supplement product label declares "black walnut (hulls)" as an ingredient, but does not declare the major food allergen “tree nuts” (specifically walnut) present in the product, as required by section 403(w)(1) of the Act. We recommend that you review your labeling to confirm that allergen declarations for all ingredients are in compliance with the requirements of section 403(w) of the Act. Please notify FDA in writing, within 15 working days of receipt of this letter, of the specific steps you have taken to address any violations. Include an explanation of each step being taken to prevent the recurrence of violations, as well as copies of related documentation. If you cannot complete corrective actions within 15 working days, state the reason for the delay and the time within which you will do so. If you believe that your products are not in violation of the Act, include your reasoning and any supporting information for our consideration. Your written reply should be directed to Rebecca Allen, United States Food and Drug Administration, Human Foods Program, Office of Enforcement, 5001 Campus Drive, College Park, Maryland 20740-3835 or via email at HFP-OCE-DietarySupplements@fda.hhs.gov. Please reference CMS #734317 on any submissions and within the subject line of any emails to us. If you have any questions, you may email at HFP-OCE-DietarySupplements@fda.hhs.gov.

issuing_office: Division Of Northeast Import
subject: Foreign Supplier Verification Program (FSVP)
text: Dear Mr. Samuel Garcia: On March 30, 2026 through April 22, 2026, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) conducted a Foreign Supplier Verification Program (FSVP) inspection of Carive Imports Inc., located at 1251 Randall Ave, Bronx, NY 10474-6411. We also conducted inspections on August 24, 2017, September 27, 2018, March 10, 2020, and June 21, 2022 through July 8, 2022. These inspections were conducted to determine compliance with the requirements of section 805 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (21 U.S.C.384a) and the implementing FSVP regulation in 21 CFR part 1, subpart L. The FSVP regulation requires that importers perform certain risk-based activities to verify that human and/or animal food they import into the United States has been produced in a manner that meets applicable U.S. food safety standards. You may find information relating to the FSVP regulation and your responsibilities to comply with the regulation through links in FDA’s FSVP web page at https://www.fda.gov/food/food-safetymodernization-act-fsma/fsma-final-rule-foreign-supplier-verification-programs-fsvp-importers-foodhumans-and-animals. During the most recent inspection, we found that you are not in compliance with the requirements of 21 CFR part 1, subpart L for the foods you import. Because of these significant violations, you are not in compliance with section 805 of the FD&C Act. At the conclusion of the inspection, our investigator provided you with a Form FDA 483a FSVP Observations. We have not received your response to the Form FDA 483a issued on April 22, 2026. Your significant violations of the FSVP regulation are as follows: If requested in writing by FDA, you must send records to the Agency electronically or through another means that delivers the records promptly, rather than making the records available for review at your place of business, as required by 21 CFR 1.510(b)(3). On March 30, 2026, our Investigator provided you with a Form FDA 482d Request for FSVP Records and spoke with you by telephone. In that conversation, you stated you would send your FSVP records. Additionally, our Investigator contacted you multiple times by email between April 2 and April 21, 2026. However, you failed to send records electronically or through another means after receiving our request in writing. As of the date of this letter, we have not received any records from you including FSVP documents for any of the foods you import, including: garlic paste imported from (b)(4) located in (b)(4) cookies imported from (b)(4) located in (b)(4) noodles imported from (b)(4) located in (b)(4) pigeon peas imported from (b)(4) located in (b)(4) The above violations are not intended to be an all-inclusive list of violations of the FSVP requirements. It is your responsibility to ensure that you are in compliance with section 805 of the FD&C Act and the implementing regulation in 21 CFR part 1, subpart L. This letter notifies you of our concerns and provides you with an opportunity to address them. If you do not adequately address this matter, we may take further action. For instance, we may take action under section 801(a)(3) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 381(a)(3)) to refuse admission of the food you import for which you appear to be in violation of section 805. We may place the foods you import into the United States on detention without physical examination (DWPE) when you import the foods. You can find DWPE information relating to FSVP in Import Alert # 99-41 at http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/cms_ia/ialist.html. In addition, the importation or offering for importation into the United States of an article of food without the importer having an FSVP that meets the requirements of section 805 of the FD&C Act or the FSVP regulation is prohibited under section 301(zz) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 331(zz)). You should respond in writing within fifteen (15) working days from your receipt of this letter. Your response should address the specific things you are doing to correct any violations. You should include in your response documentation and information that would assist us in evaluating your corrections (e.g., documentation of changes you made, such as a copy of your FSVP, records to demonstrate implementation of your FSVP), and any additional information that you wish to supply relevant to your compliance with the FSVP regulation. If you believe that you are not in violation of the FD&C Act, include your reasoning and any supporting information for our consideration. If you cannot complete all corrections within 15 working days, you should explain the reason for your delay and state when you will correct any remaining violations. Please send your reply to Food and Drug Administration, Attention: Jananiga Vanniyasingam, Compliance Officer, Division of Northeast Imports: oiioiodneiwlresponses@fda.hhs.gov. Please also cc (carbon copy) Jananiga.vanniyasingam@fda.hhs.gov. If you have any questions regarding this letter, you may contact Compliance Officer Vanniyasingam via email at ananiga.vanniyasingam@fda.hhs.gov. Please reference CMS # 730156 on any documents or records you provide to us and on the subject line of any email correspondence you send to us.

issuing_office: Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER)
subject: Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) for Nonclinical Laboratory Studies
text: Dear Mr. Rubin: This Warning Letter informs you of objectionable conditions observed during the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) inspection conducted at Lovelace Biomedical Research Institute (LBRI) between April 7 and 18, 2025. The investigator representing FDA reviewed the role of LBRI as the testing facility for the following nonclinical laboratory studies: Protocol (b)(4): “(b)(4),” of the investigational drug (b)(4), performed for (b)(4) Protocol (b)(4): “(b)(4),” of the investigational drug (b)(4), performed for (b)(4) This inspection was conducted as a part of FDA’s Bioresearch Monitoring Program, which includes inspections designed to evaluate the conduct of research and to help ensure the quality and integrity of study data, in accordance with Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations, part 58 (21 CFR 58), Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) for Nonclinical Laboratory Studies. At the conclusion of the inspection, the FDA investigator presented and discussed with you the Form FDA 483, Inspectional Observations. We acknowledge receipt of your May 9, 2025, written response to the Form FDA 483. From our review of the FDA Establishment Inspection Report, the documents submitted with that report, and your written response dated May 9, 2025, it appears that you did not adhere to the applicable statutory requirements in the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) and applicable regulations contained in 21 CFR 58 governing the conduct of nonclinical laboratory studies. We wish to emphasize the following: Failure of the quality assurance unit (QAU) to review the final study report to [en]sure that the reported results accurately reflect the raw data of the nonclinical laboratory study [21 CFR 58.35(b)(6)]. The QAU must review the final study report to ensure that the reported results accurately reflect the raw data of the nonclinical laboratory study. The QAU at your testing facility did not adhere to these requirements. Specifically, for Protocol (b)(4), the following observations found in the raw data were not documented in the final study report: 1. For 20 out of 34 animals, the final study report did not include all the abnormal cageside clinical observations that were documented between October 1 and January 3, 2024, including but not limited to sneezing; runny or bloody nose; liquid, loose, mucoid, or semisolid stool; sunken eyes; swollen perineum; bloating; hunched posture; low appetite; and heavy breathing. 2. The final study report did not include descriptions of the following dosing issues, which were recorded on the raw data forms for Intravenous Dosing and Blood Collection: a. Animal 3002, during dosing on October 16, 2023, laid on the cage bottom for one hour and ten minutes after infusion of the test article. b. Animals 3004 and 3005, during dosing on October 16, 2023, pulled out their venous catheters during infusion of the test article. c. Animals 1003 and 1004, during dosing on November 1, 2023, pulled out their venous catheters during infusion of the control article. d. Animal 4005, during dosing on November 11, 2023, had infiltration of the test article into the surrounding tissue of the left saphenous vein. Specifically, for Protocol (b)(4), the following concerns and observations noted in the raw data were not documented in the final study report: 3. The final study report did not include all the abnormal cageside clinical observations for all 48 animals, documented between November 21, 2022, and July 13, 2023, including incidences of abnormal stool observations, such as bloody or dark-red, liquid, loose, mucoid, or unformed stools. 4. The final study report did not include descriptions of the following dosing issues, which were recorded on the raw data forms for Inhalation Exposure and PK Blood Collection: a. Animal 2006, during dosing on January 10, 2023, had irregular breathing from the aerosol dosing system during the last few minutes of dosing. b. Animal 5008, during dosing on April 2, 2023, had irregular breathing and was removed from the aerosol dosing system intermittently. c. Animal 2004, during dosing on April 5, 2023, had irregular breathing and was removed from the aerosol dosing system after the first 30 minutes of the dose exposure. d. Animal 3004, on June 14, 2023, was not dosed due to a swollen muzzle. We acknowledge that this finding as described above was not included on the Form FDA 483 you received, and therefore your written response did not directly address the violation as discussed in this letter. In your May 9, 2025, written response to the Form FDA 483, regarding the abnormal cageside clinical observations, you stated that documentation of the review of Animal Management System records would be added to the study file, and an addendum would be added to the final study reports for Protocols (b)(4) and (b)(4) by May 31, 2025. You also stated that SOP-1106 (Preparation of a Final Report) and SOP-1882 (Animal Records and Animal Study Data Maintained at LBRI) would be updated by June 15, 2025. Regarding the individual dosing-related issues, your written response acknowledged that the final reports did not specifically discuss individual dosing issues. You stated that documentation of the review of those issues would be added to the study file and an addendum would be added to the final reports, as appropriate, by May 31, 2025. We acknowledge receipt of the revised final study reports, both of which were dated May 30, 2025. While we acknowledge the corrective and preventive actions that your testing facility has taken and plans to take, your response is inadequate because you did not include sufficient details about your corrective action plan. Specifically, you did not provide sufficient details regarding the updated SOPs, including the nature of the proposed or completed updates. Your corrective action plan also did not include any training on the updated SOPs or on FDA regulations governing the conduct of nonclinical laboratory studies, including the QAU’s role and responsibilities. In addition, the revised final study reports did not completely address the individual dosing issues. Finally, your corrective action plan did not include a description of any planned audits to check for compliance with updated procedures, as applicable. Without these details, we are unable to determine whether your corrective actions are adequate to prevent similar violations in the future. Because the testing facility’s QAU failed to ensure that the reported results in the final study report accurately reflected the raw data of the nonclinical laboratory studies, FDA is concerned about the integrity of the data generated and reported from nonclinical studies conducted at your testing facility. We emphasize that as a testing facility conducting nonclinical laboratory studies under 21 CFR 58, you are responsible for ensuring that nonclinical laboratory studies submitted to FDA are conducted and reported in accordance with FDA regulations to ensure the quality and integrity of study data. Your failure to conduct and report nonclinical studies in accordance with FDA regulations raises concerns about the validity and integrity of the data collected at your site. This letter is not intended to be an all-inclusive list of deficiencies with the nonclinical laboratory studies of investigational drugs conducted at your testing facility. It is your responsibility to ensure adherence to each requirement of the law and relevant FDA regulations. You should address any deficiencies and establish procedures to ensure that any ongoing or future studies comply with FDA regulations. This letter notifies you of our findings and provides you with an opportunity to address the deficiencies noted above. Within 15 business days of your receipt of this letter, you should notify this office in writing of the actions you have taken to prevent similar violations in the future. Failure to address this matter adequately may lead to regulatory action without further notice to you. If you believe that you have complied with the FD&C Act and relevant regulations, please include your reasoning and any supporting information for our consideration. Your written response, as well as any questions or concerns about this letter or the inspection, should be sent via email to the FDA at CDER-OSI-Communications@fda.hhs.gov.

issuing_office: Human Foods Program
subject: CGMP/Food/Prepared, Packed or Held Under Insanitary Conditions/Adulterated
text: Dear Ms. Lin: The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) inspected your food manufacturing facility located at 99 Atkinson St, Boston, MA 02118-2701, from March 17, 2026 through April 7, 2026. Your firm manufactures ready-to-eat (RTE) rice noodles and RTE tofu. During our inspection, the FDA investigators found serious violations of the Current Good Manufacturing Practice, Hazard Analysis, and Risk-Based Preventive Controls for Human Food regulation (CGMP & PC rule), Title 21, Code of Federal Regulations, Part 117 (21 CFR Part 117). Based on FDA’s inspectional findings, we have determined that the RTE rice noodle and tofu products manufactured in your facility are adulterated within the meaning of section 402(a)(4) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (the Act) [21 United States Code, (U.S.C.) § 342(a)(4)] in that they were prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby they may have become contaminated with filth or whereby they may have been rendered injurious to health. Additionally, the failure of the owner, operator, or agent in charge of a covered facility to comply with the preventive controls provisions of the CGMP & PC rule (located in Subparts A, C, D, E, F, and G of Part 117) is prohibited by section 301(uu) of the Act [21 U.S.C. § 331(uu)]. You may find the Act and further information about the CGMP & PC rule through links on FDA’s homepage at www.fda.gov. At the conclusion of the inspection, the FDA investigators issued a Form FDA 483 (FDA-483), Inspectional Observations, listing deviations found at your facility. We received your written response to the FDA-483 on April 28, 2026, describing your planned and implemented corrective actions. Based on our review of the inspectional findings and your response, we are issuing this letter to advise you of FDA’s continuing concerns and to provide detailed information describing the findings at your facility. We discuss your response below. Hazard Analysis and Risk-Based Preventive Controls (21 CFR part 117, Subpart C): 1. You did not conduct a hazard analysis to identify and evaluate known or reasonably foreseeable hazards for each type of food manufactured, processed, packed, or held at your facility to determine whether there are any hazards requiring a preventive control, as required by 21 CFR 117.130(a)(1). You did not conduct and document a hazard analysis for any of the foods that you manufacture. For example: A. You did not identify and evaluate the hazard of bacterial pathogen growth and/or toxin formation of Clostridium botulinum (C. botulinum) and Bacillus cereus (B. cereus) due to time/temperature abuse as a hazard requiring a preventive control for your RTE Ho Foon Cut rice noodles. C. botulinum Your RTE Ho Foon Cut rice noodle products are packaged and stored in reduced oxygen packaging (ROP). Various ingredients in these products (b)(4) grow in the ground or are associated with soil, where spores of C. botulinum may be present. Your practice of (b)(4) packing the rice noodles into impermeable bags and then squeezing the bags to remove air before tying and sealing produces an anaerobic environment. Therefore, C. botulinum growth and/or toxin formation in ROP is a known or reasonably foreseeable hazard for this product at the cooling and cold storage steps. B. cereus B. cereus is a spore-forming bacterium commonly found in soil and raw agricultural commodities, such as rice. While cooking effectively destroys its vegetative cells, the spores are notably heat-resistant and can survive standard cooking processes. Therefore, B. cereus growth and/or toxin formation is a known or reasonably foreseeable hazard for this product at the cooling and cold storage steps. You do not formulate your products (e.g., by decreasing pH or water activity) to prevent pathogen growth and/or toxin formation. Also, your (b)(4) process (observed during the inspection as approximately (b)(4) thermometer set at (b)(4) is not adequate to destroy spore-forming bacteria. If your rice noodles are time/temperature abused, bacterial spores (such as C. botulinum and B. cereus) could germinate into vegetative cells, grow, and form toxins that may lead to foodborne illness. Therefore, a knowledgeable person manufacturing/processing food in your circumstances would identify bacterial growth and/or toxin formation by spore-formers due to time/temperature abuse as a hazard requiring a preventive control at the cooling and cold storage steps. Your facility has not established preventive controls, such as process controls, for these hazards. Process controls include written procedures, practices, and processes to ensure the control of parameters during operations. Such controls could include formulation, heat processing, cooling within appropriate timeframes and/or refrigeration. Process controls must include the parameters associated with the control of the hazard, and the minimum or maximum values to which any parameter must be controlled to significantly minimize or prevent the hazards (see 21 CFR 117.135(c)(1)). An appropriate preventive control would also be subject to preventive control management components, including monitoring, corrective actions, and verification to ensure control of the hazard of bacterial growth and/or toxin formation due to time/temperature abuse for pathogens such as C. botulinum and B. cereus (see 21 CFR 117.140(a)). We have concerns about time/temperature abuse of this product in your facility. Specifically, your packaged Ho Foon Cut rice noodles are placed into the (b)(4) within (b)(4) of production for (b)(4) at approximately 5:00 PM where the noodles are stored for approximately (b)(4). On March 17, 2026, FDA investigators observed that (b)(4) separate batches of Ho Foon Cut rice noodles manufactured at (b)(4) did not sufficiently cool in the freezer, with product temperatures decreasing from 76°F (24°C) to 62 – 66°F (17–19°C) over approximately 5 hours. Furthermore, you do not monitor the temperature of your refrigerated cooler during storage. Your use of ROP for finished products is concerning based on the time-temperature abuse observed during our inspection. ROP should not be used unless appropriate barriers to Clostridium botulinum growth and toxin formation are implemented. FDA recommends referencing our Hazard Analysis and Risk-Based Preventive Controls for Human Foods: Draft Guidance for Industry and utilizing Chapter 4: Preventive Controls in the Hazard Analysis and Risk-Based Preventive Controls for Human Foods: Draft Guidance for Industry to identify suitable control measures for growth and toxin formation of Bacillus cereus and Clostridium botulinum. Additionally, Appendix 3, Table 3-A provides limiting conditions for pathogen growth that can be applied to control relevant hazards through product formulation. B. You did not identify and evaluate the hazard of vegetative bacterial pathogen survival of a lethal treatment as a hazard requiring a preventive control for your RTE Ho Foon Cut rice noodles. Your facility manufactures RTE Ho Foon Cut rice noodle products by (b)(4) your rice noodles. Vegetative bacterial pathogens have been associated with rice and rice-based noodles. Therefore, vegetative bacterial pathogens are a known or reasonably foreseeable hazard in manufacturing rice noodles. If the rice noodles are underprocessed, vegetative bacterial pathogens could survive. Therefore, a knowledgeable person manufacturing/processing food in your circumstances would identify pathogen survival of a lethal treatment as a hazard requiring a preventive control. Your facility has not established preventive controls, such as process controls, for these hazards. Process controls include written procedures, practices, and processes to ensure the control of parameters during operations (b)(4). Process controls must include the parameters associated with the control of the hazard and the minimum and maximum values needed to significantly minimize or prevent the hazards (see 21 CFR 117.135(c)(1)). An appropriate preventive control would also be subject to preventive control management components, including monitoring, corrective actions, and verification to ensure control of the hazard of vegetative bacterial pathogen survival of a lethal treatment. We have concerns that you are not eliminating vegetative pathogens in your rice noodles during the (b)(4) process. On March 19, 2026, during production of RTE Ho Foon Cut rice noodles packaged in 2 lb. bags, investigators found that the rice noodle mixture entered the (b)(4) at an internal product temperature of 57°F (14°C) and exited the (b)(4) after 56 seconds at 149°F (65°C). Furthermore, you have not conducted a validation study demonstrating that your process will adequately destroy vegetative bacterial pathogens (see 21 CFR 117.160.) C. You did not identify and evaluate recontamination with environmental pathogens as a hazard requiring a preventive control for your RTE Ho Foon Cut rice noodles and tofu products. Your facility manufactures Ho Foon Cut rice noodle products and tofu, which are RTE and exposed to the environment after cooking and prior to packaging. Therefore, contamination with environmental pathogens is a known or reasonably foreseeable hazard. The packaged foods do not receive any further lethal treatment or otherwise include a control measure that would significantly minimize the pathogen. Therefore, a knowledgeable person manufacturing/processing food in your circumstances would identify contamination with environmental pathogens as a hazard requiring a preventive control. Preventive controls include sanitation controls, which include procedures, practices, and processes to ensure that the facility is maintained in a sanitary condition adequate to significantly minimize or prevent hazards such as environmental pathogens and biological hazards due to employee handling (see 21 CFR 117.135(c)(3)). Although your facility maintains a written sanitation program titled “Equipment Sanitation Doc# EQ-001 Ver. 3.0” with an effective date of 2/1/2025, it does not include: cleaning/sanitation procedures for the tofu line, procedures related to employee practices and hand hygiene, and preventive control management components. Preventive controls are subject to preventive control management components (monitoring, verification, and corrective actions) as appropriate to ensure the effectiveness of the preventive controls, taking into account the nature of the preventive control and its role in the facility’s food safety system (see 21 CFR 117.140). In addition, you did not have adequate controls in place for contamination with environmental pathogens, as evidenced by the following observations during the inspection on March 17 and 18, 2026: Cleaning and sanitation of equipment • On March 18, 2026, the production manager stated he had verified the (b)(4) sanitizer concentration (b)(4) prior to use on food-contact surfaces for manufacturing RTE Ho Foon Cut rice noodles. However, investigators observed him measuring the sanitizer concentration at approximately 100 ppm with a test strip. Your production manager did not follow the (b)(4) sanitizer’s instructions for use or your “Equipment Sanitation Doc #: EQ-001” procedure, which specified the sanitizer concentration of (b)(4), and required documentation of the sanitizer strength on “Attachment 4”. Your firm then manufactured rice noodles on this equipment where RTE products came in direct contact on March 19, 2026. • On March 18, 2026, during post-manufacturing sanitation of RTE Ho Foon Cut rice noodles equipment, investigators observed residual noodles remaining on food-contact surfaces (e.g. (b)(4) on the line (b)(4) conveyor) in (b)(4) areas, after the sanitation crew completed cleaning but before sanitizer application. Employee practices • An employee wearing rubber gloves draped a red water hose (a portion of which routinely touched the floor) over the frame of the tofu press, then used a scoop to transfer RTE tofu into drain molds. The scoop, including the handle, was placed inside the RTE tofu in the drain mold. The employee did not wash or sanitize their hands or change their gloves between these activities. • An employee touched a floor dolly, then a yellow basket holding drain cloths (to be washed), and then picked up a knife to cut RTE tofu into cubes. The employee then picked up the drain tray containing RTE tofu and (b)(4) placed the cubed RTE tofu into the cooling bath. The employee did not wash or sanitize their hands or change their gloves between these activities. • An employee returned from break and did not wash or sanitize their hands before removing plastic containers and lids (primary packaging) from bags in cardboard boxes and placing them on the table or in a plastic crate. The employee was routinely touching the food-contact surfaces of the containers. These containers and lids were then used for packaging of the silken tofu lot # (b)(4). • An employee handled a blue floor pallet routinely stored in the firm's cooler (used for holding packaged RTE tofu) and placed it by the tofu packaging table. The employee only rinsed their hands with water (no soap), put on gloves and (b)(4) packaged RTE silken tofu lot (b)(4). D. You did not identify and evaluate undeclared allergens due to incorrect labeling as a hazard requiring a preventive control. Your Ho Foon Cut Noodles include (b)(4) as an ingredient. Therefore, undeclared allergens due to incorrect labeling is a known or reasonably foreseeable hazard, and a knowledgeable person manufacturing/processing food in your circumstances would identify the hazard as requiring a preventive control at the bagging/labeling step. Preventive controls, such as allergen or process controls, include written procedures, practices, and processes for labeling the finished food to control food allergens, including by ensuring that the finished food is not misbranded under section 403(w) of the Act (see 21 CFR 117.135(c)(2)). You do not have written allergen control procedures, including monitoring, corrective action and verification to ensure control of the hazard of undeclared allergens due to incorrect labeling. Your response to the FDA-483 dated April 28, 2026 stated that you have reached out to a new consultant to assist in the development of a Food Safety Plan, that you have scheduled PCQI training, and that you are working on finding ways that will work with your production process and limited freezer space to help cool down the Ho Foon noodles in the appropriate timeframe. You stated that you are also researching companies that provide in-person food safety training in multiple languages for employees. However, to date, you have not provided additional information or other substantive documents to the Agency regarding these issues. Current Good Manufacturing Practice (21 CFR Part 117, Subpart B) 1. Your plant was not constructed in such a manner so that floors may be adequately cleaned and kept clean and kept in good repair, and that drip condensate from fixtures, ducts and pipes does not contaminate food and food-contact surfaces, as required by 21 CFR 117.20(b)(4). Specifically, • Condensate was observed on the overhead water pipe directly above the RTE tofu packaging table, and droplets were observed on the food-contact surfaces of the primary packaging including lids and containers used to package Silken Tofu lot #(b)(4). • Condensate from the water line and on/off valve was dripping directly into the tofu cooling bath. The cooling bath was filled with water, and cubed tofu lot # (b)(4) was placed directly in the water for cooling. • The floor in the production area where RTE tofu is processed and packaged had missing cement and exposed aggregate. Your response to the FDA-483 dated April 28, 2026 stated that you have resurfaced and epoxied the floor of the tofu production area, with photographs. Your response did not address drip condensate. We will verify the adequacy of your corrective actions during a future inspection of your facility. The violations cited in this letter are not intended to be an all-inclusive list of the violations that exist at your facility or in connection with your products. You are responsible for investigating and determining the causes of any violations and for preventing their recurrence or the occurrence of other violations. It is your responsibility to ensure that your firm complies with all requirements of federal law, including applicable FDA regulations. This letter notifies you of our concerns and provides you an opportunity to address them. Failure to adequately address this matter may result in legal action including, without limitation, seizure and injunction. Please notify FDA in writing within fifteen (15) working days of receipt of this letter of the specific steps you have taken to address any violations. Include an explanation of each step being taken to prevent the recurrence of violations, as well as copies of related documentation. If you cannot complete corrective actions within fifteen (15) working days, state the reason for the delay and the time within which you will do so. If you believe that your products are not in violation of the Act, include your reasoning and any supporting information for our consideration. Please send your reply to: HFP-OCE-ConventionalFoods@fda.hhs.gov, copying Elodie Tong-Lin, Compliance Officer at elodie.tong-lin@fda.hhs.gov. If you have any questions regarding this letter, you may contact Elodie Tong-Lin, Compliance Officer, via email at elodie.tong-lin@fda.hhs.gov. text: Dear Mr. Jeffrey Stevens: This is to advise you that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) reviewed your website at the Internet address www.psyched-wellness.com in May 2026 and has determined that you take orders there for various human food products, which you represent as containing Amanita muscaria. FDA has determined that your products, Calm, Calmer, and Santa, are adulterated under section 402(f)(1)(B) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (the Act), 21 U.S.C. 342(f)(1)(B). As explained further below, introducing or delivering these products for introduction into interstate commerce for such uses violates the Act. You can find the Act and FDA regulations through links on FDA’s home page at www.fda.gov. Adulterated Dietary Supplements The labeling of your Calm, Calmer, and Santa products declares Amanita muscaria extract as a dietary ingredient. Based on a review of your product labeling, the Amanita muscaria extract in your Calm, Calmer, and Santa products is a “dietary ingredient” under section 201(ff)(1)(F) of the Act (21 U.S.C. 321(ff)(1)(F)). Amanita muscaria, A. muscaria extract, ibotenic acid, muscarine, and muscimol are new dietary ingredients under section 413(d) of the Act (21 U.S.C. 350b(d)) because, to the best of FDA’s knowledge, there is no information demonstrating that Amanita muscaria was marketed as a dietary ingredient in the United States before October 15, 1994. A dietary supplement is adulterated under section 402(f)(1)(B) of the Act (21 U.S.C. 342(f)(1)(B)) of the Act if it contains a new dietary ingredient for which there is inadequate information to provide reasonable assurance that such ingredient does not present a significant or unreasonable risk of illness or injury. Based on our evaluation of the relevant safety evidence, there is inadequate information to provide reasonable assurance that Amanita muscaria does not present a significant or unreasonable risk of illness or injury. Therefore, your dietary supplements containing Amanita muscaria are adulterated under section 402(f)(1)(B) of the Act. The introduction of such adulterated dietary supplements into interstate commerce is prohibited under section 301(a) of the Act. Moreover, available information on the use of Amanita muscaria in products raises serious safety concerns. This letter is not intended to be an all-inclusive statement of violations that may exist in connection with your products. You are responsible for investigating and determining the causes of any violations and for preventing their recurrence or the occurrence of other violations. It is your responsibility to ensure that your firm complies with all requirements of federal law, including FDA regulations. This letter notifies you of our concerns and provides you an opportunity to address them. Failure to adequately address this matter may result in legal action including, without limitation, seizure and injunction. Please notify FDA in writing, within 15 working days of receipt of this letter, of the specific steps you have taken to address any violations. Include an explanation of each step being taken to prevent the recurrence of violations, as well as copies of related documentation. If you cannot complete corrective actions within 15 working days, state the reason for the delay and the time within which you will do so. If you believe that your products are not in violation of the Act, include your reasoning and any supporting information for our consideration. Your written reply should be directed to Rebecca Allen, United States Food and Drug Administration, Human Foods Program, Office of Enforcement, 5001 Campus Drive, College Park, Maryland 20740-3835 or via email at HFP-OCE DietarySupplements@fda.hhs.gov. Please reference CMS #730137 on any submissions and within the subject line of any emails to us. If you have any questions, you may email at HFP-OCE-DietarySupplements@fda.hhs.gov.

text: Dear Ms. Ving and Mr. Ving: The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) inspected two of your Rama Food Manufacture Corp. food manufacturing facilities located at 1486 E Cedar Street, Ontario, California 91761 and 2131 S Parco Avenue, Ontario, California 91761 from January 27 through February 26, 2026. Both facilities manufacture ready-to-eat (RTE) rice noodles (various noodle sizes/types). During our inspections, FDA investigators observed serious violations of the Current Good Manufacturing Practice, Hazard Analysis, and Risk-Based Preventive Controls for Human Food regulation (CGMP & PC rule), Title 21, Code of Federal Regulations, Part 117 (21 CFR Part 117). Additionally, FDA collected environmental samples (i.e., swabs) from various areas in both facilities. FDA laboratory analysis of the environmental swabs found the presence of Listeria innocua and grayi in your S Parco Avenue facility and L. grayi in your E Cedar Street facility, which are non-human pathogenic Listeria spp. FDA also collected four finished product samples and analyzed them for water activity and pH. Based on FDA’s inspectional findings and analytical results for finished product samples of Pad Thai Rice Stick Noodle, Fresh Rice Stick Noodle Banh Pho Tuoi, and Rice Stick Noodle Big Cut Noodle, we have determined that the RTE rice noodle products manufactured in both of your facilities are adulterated within the meaning of section 402(a)(4) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (the Act) [21 U.S.C. § 342(a)(4)] because they were prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby they may have become contaminated with filth or been rendered injurious to health. In addition, failure of the owner, operator, or agent in charge of a covered facility to comply with the preventive control provisions of the CGMP & PC rule (located in subparts A, C, D, E, F, and G of Part 117) is prohibited by section 301(uu) of the Act [21 U.S.C. § 331(uu)]. You may find the Act and further information about the CGMP & PC rule through links on FDA’s website at http://www.fda.gov. At the conclusion of both inspections, the FDA investigators issued a Form FDA 483 (FDA-483), Inspectional Observations to each facility. We received your written responses to both FDA-483s on March 17, 2026, describing your planned and implemented corrective actions. Based on our review of the inspectional and analytical findings and your responses, we are issuing this letter to advise you of FDA’s continuing concerns and to provide detailed information describing the findings at each of your facilities. We discuss your responses below. Hazard Analysis and Risk-Based Preventive Controls (21 CFR Part 117, Subpart C): E Cedar Street Facility 1. Your written process preventive control procedures were not appropriate to significantly minimize or prevent hazards requiring preventive controls, as required by 21 CFR 117.135(c)(1). Your facility’s written hazard analysis determined that pathogen hazards such as Bacillus cereus (B. cereus), Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes (L. monocytogenes), and Clostridium botulinum (C. botulinum) required a preventive control. The “Preventive Controls” section of your food safety plan document indicates that such hazards will be significantly minimized or prevented at the rice (b)(4) to rice (b)(4), rice (b)(4), (b)(4), and (b)(4) processing steps. However, a review of your established control methods/critical limits for these process preventive controls determined that they may not control the hazards. Additionally, in some cases, monitoring of these parameters was not implemented and/or the parameters were not met. Specifically, a. (b)(4): Your “Temperature Control of Rice (b)(4) Tank” process preventive control covering rice (b)(4) to rice (b)(4) in your food safety plan lists a critical limit of “Rice (b)(4) Temperature ≤ (b)(4)” to be checked “Every (b)(4)” which does not provide sufficient control for the hazard of B. cereus identified at these processing steps. If the (b)(4) rice is exposed to temperatures above 70°F for more than three hours cumulatively, pathogens such as B. cereus can grow and produce toxin. FDA recommends referencing Appendix 3, Table 3-B of our Draft Guidance for Industry: Hazard Analysis and Risk-Based Preventive Controls for Human Food, which explains that for the potential hazardous conditions of growth and toxin formation of B. cereus, the recommended maximum cumulative exposure time for product temperatures above 70°F is three hours. Your response to the FDA-483 dated March 17, 2026, included updated time and temperature critical limits for the process preventive control covering the rice (b)(4) and rice (b)(4) steps (b)(4). As written, your critical limits of (b)(4) process ≤ (b)(4) rice temperature ≤ (b)(4), (b)(4) process ≤ (b)(4), and (b)(4) rice temperature ≤ (b)(4) would still allow the soaked and ground rice to be exposed to temperatures above 70°F for up to 3.5 hours cumulatively, which does not appear to provide adequate control for the hazard of B. cereus. Your response also referenced a proposed challenge study as the basis for these critical limits and stated that the results of the study would be provided upon completion. To date, you have not provided additional information to the Agency regarding this issue. b. (b)(4): Your “pH Control of Rice (b)(4)” process preventive control (b)(4) in your food safety plan lists a critical limit of “Rice (b)(4)” which may not provide sufficient control for the hazard of pathogen growth and toxin formation, such as B. cereus, identified at this processing step. Your firm stated that (b)(4) were also added to control for B. cereus; however, you had no written process preventive control for the addition of (b)(4). The rice (b)(4) is (b)(4) before being (b)(4) and packaged, exposing the noodles to elevated temperatures for extended periods of time which may allow for the growth of pathogens and/or toxin formation, such as B. cereus. On February 12, 2026, our investigators measured the temperature of in-process RTE rice noodle sheets, Lot (b)(4), from Lines (b)(4) and (b)(4) at the (b)(4) step at (b)(4) and (b)(4) around 9:20 AM. After (b)(4), the rice noodle sheets were (b)(4) approximately (b)(4). A (b)(4) was placed on the stacked sheets, and a fan was blowing on the rice sheets during the (b)(4) process. At 10:38 AM, the rice noodle sheet temperature measured at 87°F and 87.5°F. At 3:30 PM, our investigators measured the rice noodle sheet temperatures from each line at 80°F and 81.5°F, respectively. The temperatures of rice noodle sheets were above 70°F for 6 hours and 10 minutes when this process was observed during the inspection. Your response to the FDA-483 indicated the use of pH control and (b)(4) in the rice (b)(4) to control for the hazards of B. cereus and C. perfringens at “(b)(4).” However, the letter you provided from (b)(4) noted “A product-specific validation (e.g. (b)(4)) for B. cereus is recommended to specifically support the Food Safety Plan for its control in the noodle process.” You indicated that you were planning a validation study for product (b)(4) with your microbiological consultant and that you would submit the results once completed. To date, you have not provided such a validation study to the Agency. Additionally, we note that you have not identified the cooling of the cooked rice noodle sheets (b)(4) as requiring a process preventive control and have not implemented monitoring procedures to ensure the RTE rice noodle sheets are cooled quickly enough to adequately control bacterial growth and/or toxin formation during cooling. FDA recommends in the Food Code cooling from 57ºC (135ºF) to 21ºC (70°F) within 2 hours and then further cooling to 5ºC (41°F) within a total of six hours. The cooling time to reduce temperatures to 21ºC (70°F) is important to ensure products are cooled quickly through the optimum temperatures for growth of bacterial pathogens. Your response to the FDA-483 indicates that you intend the rice (b)(4) pH check and (b)(4) to provide adequate control for B. cereus growth and/or toxin formation through the noodle cooling and drying process. However, as noted above, you have not provided the results of the planned validation study referenced in your response. c. (b)(4): Your “(b)(4)” process preventive control (b)(4) in your food safety plan lists temperature checks and pH checks as control mechanisms for pathogen growth [L. monocytogenes and C. botulinum in (b)(4). For temperature checks, you list a method of “Check Finished Product temperature ((b)(4)) ≤ (b)(4)” with a frequency of “(b)(4)”. Your finished RTE rice noodles are packaged before (b)(4) without the product temperature being monitored. Most foodborne bacteria and bacterial spores can survive refrigeration, and some relevant organisms can continue growing at or below 40°F. For pH checks you list a method of “Check Finished Product pH ≤ (b)(4)” with a frequency of “(b)(4)”. (b)(4) ≤ (b)(4) alone may not be adequate for Listeria control and your products were observed to be exposed to temperatures above 40°F for extended periods of time during finished product storage after packaging, which can allow for the growth of L. monocytogenes. Additionally, FDA’s sampling results for your finished rice noodle products demonstrate that you do not consistently meet your critical limit of a pH (b)(4) in finished products (refer to Table 1 below). Also, you check the pH of (b)(4), which is not representative of the entire lot of approximately (b)(4) of rice noodles. Your firm packages RTE rice noodles (various noodle sizes/types) in 1 lb. reduced oxygen packaging (ROP), in (b)(4) lb. (b)(4) film packaging, and in (b)(4) lb. packaging where (b)(4) is (b)(4) from the package and bags are (b)(4) closed (the latter two may create ROP conditions due to permeability of the packaging material). This creates anaerobic conditions that can allow for C. botulinum growth and toxin formation in the absence of adequate product pH and temperature controls. Your control method of a finished product pH of (b)(4) may provide adequate control for the hazard of C. botulinum at this processing step if properly implemented. However, FDA collected finished product samples from your E Cedar Street facility for pH and water activity analysis. The analysis found that your process did not consistently yield a finished product pH (b)(4) in accordance with the critical limit established by your firm. The results are summarized in the table below: Table 1. FDA Sample Results- Finished Products Collected from E Cedar Street Facility FDA Sample #/ProductpH (original)/pH (check)L. monocytogenes growth supported?C. botulinum growth supported?1317729/PAD THAI Rice Stick Noodle 1lb, Lot (b)(4)4.59 to 4.75/4.55 to 4.63Yes, pH > 4.4No, however, the pH is above your firm’s target pH of (b)(4) at (b)(4) for finished products.1317730/FRESH RICE STICK NOODLE BANH PHO TUOI, 1lb Lot (b)(4)4.58 to 4.78/4.64 to 4.91Yes, pH >4.4Yes, the pH was as high as 4.91 in the check analysis, and it exceeds your firm’s target pH of (b)(4) at (b)(4) for finished products.1317732/RICE STICK NOODLE BIG CUT NOODLE 10 lbs., Lot (b)(4)4.55 to 4.61/4.55 to 4.64Yes, pH > 4.4No, however, the pH is above your firm’s target pH of (b)(4) at (b)(4) for finished products. *Note: The water activity values were above 0.85 in the RTE rice noodle samples analyzed by FDA (water activity values ranged from 0.98 to 1.00). Additionally, your temperature check control mechanism does not appear to provide adequate control for the finished product stage. For example, during the inspection our investigators observed the following: On January 28, 2026, our investigators measured temperatures between two bags from two different locations on a pallet of finished product Banh Pho Tuoi noodles, Lot (b)(4) ((b)(4) plastic ROP, (b)(4) per box), at 52°F and 53.5°F while stored in the cooler. The noodles had been cut and packaged on (b)(4), and visible condensate was observed inside the finished product packaging. On January 28, 2026, our investigators measured the temperature between two bags of finished product Pad Thai noodles, Lot (b)(4) ((b)(4) plastic ROP, (b)(4) per box), at 70.5°F while stored in the cooler. The noodles had been cut and packaged on (b)(4), and visible condensate was observed inside the finished product packaging. On February 12, 2026, cooked, in-process rice noodle sheets from Lot (b)(4), held (b)(4) Lines (b)(4), were observed stored at (b)(4) temperature. At 9:40 AM, our investigators measured the rice noodle sheet temperatures at 82°F, 77°F, and 81°F, respectively. At 3:32 PM, our investigators measured the rice noodle sheet temperatures at 79.5°F, 73°F, and 73°F, respectively. The rice noodle sheets remained at (b)(4) temperature (b)(4) until cut into individual noodles and packaged as Banh Pho Tuoi (10 lb.), Lot (b)(4), at approximately 5:30 AM and placed in the refrigerator at approximately 6:00 AM on February 13, 2026. At 9:13 AM on February 13, 2026, our investigators measured the temperature of a finished RTE 10 lb. ROP bag of Banh Pho Tuoi rice noodles in the refrigerator at 61°F. On February 23, 2026, our investigators measured the temperature between two bags of finished Banh Pho Tuoi noodles, Lot 04-23-A1 (10 lb. bags, (b)(4) and (b)(4) closed, (b)(4) bags per box), at 78.5°F at 9:10 AM. These products were placed in the cooler at approximately 9:05 AM. At 3:18 PM, our investigators measured the temperatures between the bags of finished rice noodles at 74.5°F. On February 24, 2026, at 11:10 AM, our investigators measured the temperature between the bags of finished rice noodles at 66.5°F. After 26 hours of refrigerator storage, the product had cooled by only 12°F. Packaged finished products from your firm’s S Parco Avenue facility are also stored at your E Cedar Street facility until distribution. On February 23, 2026, our investigators measured the temperature between two bags of finished Banh Pho Tuoi noodles, Lot 04-23-B1 ((b)(4) bags, (b)(4) and (b)(4) closed, (b)(4) bags per box), from the S Parco Avenue facility at 66.5°F at 9:10 AM. These products were placed in your E Cedar Street facility cooler at approximately 9:00 AM. At 3:18 PM, our investigators measured the temperatures between the bags of finished rice noodles at 66°F. On February 24, 2026, at 11:10 AM, our investigators measured the temperature between the bags of finished rice noodles at 62°F. After 26 hours of refrigerated storage, the finished product had cooled by only 4.5°F. Your FDA-483 response included an updated process preventive control of testing the pH of (b)(4); however, we are unable to fully evaluate the response because it is unclear whether (b)(4) samples is representative of the entire batch of approximately (b)(4) of rice noodles. Moreover, a pH of (b)(4) alone may not be adequate for Listeria control. FDA recommends referencing Appendix 3, Table 3-A of our Draft Guidance for Industry: Hazard Analysis and Risk-Based Preventive Controls for Human Food, which outlines the limiting conditions for L. monocytogenes growth. Additionally, your written response does not account for when the temperature of the RTE packaged rice noodles are not monitored during storage in the cooler before they are shipped, which can allow for pathogen growth and/or toxin formation in the finished product due to extended exposure to elevated temperatures over time. Your practice of not releasing product for shipment until it is (b)(4) does not provide adequate control for this hazard. As previously mentioned, most foodborne bacteria and bacterial spores can survive refrigeration, and some relevant organisms can continue growing at or below (b)(4). We acknowledge receipt of certificates of destruction for your voluntary destruction of in-process and finished products as part of the corrective actions taken by your firm in response to these observations. 2. Your written sanitation preventive controls did not include procedures, practices, and processes to ensure that the facility is maintained in a sanitary condition adequate to significantly minimize or prevent hazards such as environmental pathogens and biological hazards due to employee handling, to comply with 21 CFR 117.135(c)(3). Your food safety plan listed the hazard of “Biological” and an associated sanitation preventive control of “Cleaning of equipment and utensils.” However, your cleaning practices for your food contact equipment after the (b)(4) step are not adequate to significantly minimize or prevent hazards given the infrequent nature of the cleaning. More specifically, during the inspection, our investigators observed that you use cut machines (b)(4), noodle trays (b)(4), and cut tables (b)(4) for daily production runs, but the cleaning and sanitation is completed on a rotating basis, so equipment is cleaned and sanitized only (b)(4). This frequency does not ensure that the facility is maintained in a sanitary condition adequate to significantly minimize or prevent hazards given that your RTE rice noodle sheets and RTE cut rice noodles are exposed to the environment after being (b)(4) and (b)(4) and (b)(4) handled by employees prior to being packaged, where they may be contaminated with environmental pathogens, such as L. monocytogenes and other pathogens due to poor sanitation and employee practices. We also note that the (b)(4) sheets used in direct contact with stacked RTE rice noodle sheets during drying/curing were not being cleaned and sanitized at all. These sheets were observed with discoloration, and some sheets had frayed edges as well. Your response to the FDA-483 indicated you have updated your sanitation preventive controls by including personnel handwashing and an “EMP program” as new components. Your response also described a new equipment wipe down practice using (b)(4) in your Cutting/Packing Department and Noodle Receiving area at the (b)(4), and you noted that cleaning of electric fans and (b)(4) sheets are included in the wipe down activity for the Noodle Receiving area. We will evaluate the adequacy of your corrective actions during our next inspection. S Parco Avenue Facility 3. You did not prepare, or have prepared, and implement a food safety plan, as required by 21 CFR 117.126(a)(1). Your food safety plan must include the following: 1) The written hazard analysis, as required by § 117.130(a)(2); 2) The written preventive controls, as required by § 117.135(b); 3) The written supply‐chain program, as required by subpart G; 4) The written recall plan, as required by § 117.139(a); 5) The written procedures for monitoring the implementation of the preventive controls, as required by § 117.145(a); 6) The written corrective action procedures, as required by § 117.150(a)(1); and 7) The written verification procedures, as required by § 117.165(b). Your facility manufactures refrigerated RTE rice noodles in ROP packaging. However, you did not have a food safety plan with any of the required elements for these products. For example, you did not conduct a hazard analysis to identify and evaluate known or reasonably foreseeable hazards for RTE rice noodles manufactured and packaged at your facility to determine whether there are any hazards requiring a preventive control, as required by 21 CFR 117.130(a). Also, you did not identify and implement preventive controls to provide assurances that any hazards requiring a preventive control will be significantly minimized or prevented and the food manufactured, processed, packed, or held by your facility will not be adulterated under section 402 of the Act [see 21 CFR 117.135(a)(1)]. Preventive controls include, as appropriate to the facility and the food, process controls, food allergen controls, sanitation controls, supply-chain controls, and a recall plan [see 21 CFR 117.135(c)]. Preventive controls are subject to preventive control management components (monitoring, verification, and corrective actions) as appropriate to ensure the effectiveness of the preventive controls, taking into account the nature of the preventive control and its role in the facility's food safety system (see 21 CFR 117.140). For example, you did not identify growth and survival of bacterial pathogens, such as B. cereus, L. monocytogenes, and C. botulinum as known or reasonably foreseeable hazards to determine whether they are hazards requiring a preventive control. Your in-process and finished ROP rice noodles are produced without time-temperature and/or (b)(4) and are likely to support the growth of bacterial pathogens and/or toxin formation. A knowledgeable person manufacturing/processing food in your circumstances would identify growth of bacterial pathogens as a hazard requiring a preventive control (e.g., process controls). Process controls include procedures, practices, and processes to ensure the control of parameters during operations. Where appropriate, process controls must also include the parameters associated with the control of the hazard and the minimum and/or maximum values needed to significantly minimize or prevent the hazards requiring a process control [see 21 CFR 117.135(c)(1)]. During the inspection, FDA investigators observed the following instances of time-temperature abuse of the RTE rice noodles: On February 11, 2026, our investigators measured the temperature of cooked in-process RTE Banh Pho Tuoi rice noodle sheets, Lot (b)(4), during the (b)(4) process on Lines (b)(4) and (b)(4) at 9:00 AM at 69°F and 66.5°F, respectively. The rice noodle sheets were stacked (b)(4) sheets in stacks approximately four feet high with a (b)(4) of each stack. At 10:14 AM the temperature of the rice noodle sheets was measured at 71.5°F and 64.5°F; at 12:19 PM the temperature was measured at 69°F and 65°F; and at 3:20 PM, was measured at 69°F and 66°F. The cut noodles are packed in 10 lb. bags with the (b)(4) removed and (b)(4) closed creating the potential for ROP conditions within the bag due to the permeability of the packaging material. The bags are packed in cases, the cases are palletized and wrapped in plastic wrap, and the pallets are transferred from the S Parco facility to the refrigerator at the E Cedar facility before being fully cooled. As noted in the E Cedar facility observations above, Lot 04-23-B1 of Banh Pho Tuoi noodles cooled by only 4.5°F over 26 hours (from 66.5°F to 62°F). Further, FDA sample (#1317731) of refrigerated FRESH RICE STICK NOODLE BANH PHO TUOI (10 lbs., Lot (b)(4)) was collected and analyzed for pH and water activity. The finished product was found to have a pH range of 4.67 to 4.93 (original analysis) and 4.52 to 4.64 (check analysis). The water activity was found to be 1.0 (original analysis) and 0.99 (check analysis). These pH and water activity values may allow for bacterial pathogen growth and toxin formation. Additionally, you did not identify recontamination with environmental pathogens, such as L. monocytogenes, as a known or reasonably foreseeable hazard to determine whether it is a hazard requiring a preventive control. Your RTE rice noodles are exposed to the environment after being (b)(4) and (b)(4) dried and then (b)(4) by employees prior to packaging. The packaged noodles do not receive a lethal treatment or otherwise include another control that would significantly minimize the hazard of recontamination with environmental pathogens. Contamination with environmental pathogens is a known or reasonably foreseeable hazard. A knowledgeable person manufacturing/processing food in your circumstances would identify contamination with environmental pathogens as a hazard requiring a preventive control (e.g., sanitation controls). Sanitation controls include procedures, practices, and processes to ensure that the facility is maintained in a sanitary condition adequate to significantly minimize or prevent hazards such as environmental pathogens and biological hazards due to employee handling [see 21 CFR 117.135(c)(3)]. In addition, we note that verification activities must include, as appropriate, environmental monitoring if contamination of an RTE food with an environmental pathogen is a hazard requiring a preventive control [see 21 CFR 117.165(a)(3)]. Your firm’s FDA-483 response dated March 17, 2026 provided a hazard analysis and preventive controls and an environmental monitoring program. We acknowledge that you intend to use pH, (b)(4), and temperature controls to ensure the safety of your finished RTE rice noodle products. However, your process preventive controls for the manufacturing of RTE rice noodles at your S Parco Avenue facility appear to be the same as those provided for your E Cedar Street facility. Accordingly, FDA has the same concerns regarding inadequate controls for bacterial pathogen growth and/or toxin formation as those discussed above for the E Cedar Street facility. We also note that the food safety plan, dated March 9, 2026 included in your FDA-483 response did not include a written recall plan as required. Current Good Manufacturing Practice (21 CFR Part 117, Subpart B): E Cedar Street Facility 1. Your plant was not constructed in such a manner that drip or condensate from fixtures, ducts and pipes does not contaminate food and food-contact surfaces, as required by 21 CFR 117.20(b)(4). Specifically, on January 27, 2026, during the manufacturing of RTE rice noodle sheets (Lot (b)(4)), continuous (b)(4) around the (b)(4) vent hoods on (b)(4) Lines (b)(4) and (b)(4) were observed, with condensate collecting on the edge of the (b)(4) exhaust hoods directly over exposed noodle sheets. Condensate was observed to drip from the hood surface which is located at the (b)(4). The exterior surface of the (b)(4) hood on Line (b)(4) was observed with rust-like discoloration on the outer hood surface where condensate was forming. Your response to the FDA-483 indicated that the (b)(4) vent hood was thoroughly cleaned and sanitized to prevent condensation and to remove rust. Your response is not adequate because it does not address how you would prevent condensate from forming and serving as a potential contaminant to food-contact surfaces and to your RTE rice noodle products (b)(4) the (b)(4) in the future. S Parco Avenue Facility 2. You did not clean and sanitize your utensils and equipment in a manner that protects against contamination of food-contact surfaces, as required by 21 CFR 117.35(a). During cleaning and sanitation operations on January 29, 2026 in your S Parco facility, FDA investigators observed employees cleaning soiled equipment in a manner that caused overspray to contact food-contact surfaces of equipment that had already been cleaned. Your response to the FDA-483 indicated that personnel were trained to avoid recontamination of cleaned equipment by avoiding splashing water. We will evaluate the adequacy of your corrective action during the next inspection of your facility. 3. You did not take effective measures to exclude pests from the manufacturing, processing, packing, and holding areas of your facility to protect against contamination of food, as required by 21 CFR 117.35(c). Specifically, a. On January 27, 2026, during the manufacturing of RTE Banh Pho Tuoi rice noodles (Lot (b)(4)), at least five apparent dead black winged insects were observed in (b)(4) and one bee-like insect was observed on the dispensing table adjacent to the (b)(4) bulk tote. Two live black winged insects were observed on a (b)(4) bag holding rice. b. On February 5, 2026, during the manufacturing of RTE Banh Pho Tuoi rice noodles (Lot (b)(4)), two dead apparent cockroaches were observed in the facility. One insect was observed in the drain between the rice noodle (b)(4) lines, and one was observed between pallets of raw rice. Your response to the FDA-483 addressed actions taken by your pest control company to treat for cockroaches and actions you have taken to prevent their entry into the facility. An employee training record covering the requirement for personnel to report pest sightings in the production facility was also provided and focused on cockroaches and mouse/rat activity. We note that the (b)(4) rice observed in contact with dead black winged insects was voluntarily discarded on January 27, 2026, following identification of this condition. We will evaluate the adequacy of your corrective actions during the next inspection. This letter is not intended to be an all-inclusive statement of violations that may exist at your facility or in connection with your products. You are responsible for investigating and determining the causes of any violations and for preventing their recurrence or the occurrence of other violations. It is your responsibility to ensure that your firm complies with all requirements of federal law, including applicable FDA regulations. This letter notifies you of our concerns and provides you an opportunity to address them. Failure to adequately address this matter may result in legal action including, without limitation, seizure and injunction. We also offer the following comments: On February 3, 2026, FDA collected environmental swabs (FDA sample #1309377) from your E Cedar Street facility. Two (2) swabs collected from a (b)(4) tested positive for Listeria grayi. This (b)(4) was approximately (b)(4) area and approximately (b)(4). On February 10, 2026, FDA collected environmental swabs (FDA sample #1322596) from your S Parco Avenue facility. Two (2) swabs tested positive for Listeria innocua (including the food contact surface of the (b)(4) above the (b)(4) and the (b)(4) and two (2) locations were positive for Listeria grayi (b)(4) on the (b)(4). These findings can be an indicator of inadequate sanitation and of conditions that support the growth of Listeria monocytogenes (a human pathogen) in your manufacturing facilities. We acknowledge the presence of cooking instructions on your product labeling and your work in establishing the adequacy of these instructions, however your rice noodles are a RTE food as it is reasonably foreseeable that your fully cooked rice noodles will be eaten without further processing that would significantly minimize biological hazards based on how consumers use your product. Please notify FDA in writing, within fifteen (15) working days of receipt of this letter, of the specific steps you have taken to address any violations. Include an explanation of each step being taken to prevent the recurrence of violations, as well as copies of related documentation. If you cannot complete corrective actions within fifteen (15) working days, state the reason for the delay and the time within which you will do so. If you believe that your products are not in violation of the Act, include your reasoning and any supporting information for our consideration. Please send your reply to: HFP-OCE-ConventionalFoods@fda.hhs.gov, copying Valerie Potopsingh, Compliance Officer at valerie.potopsingh@fda.hhs.gov or by hardcopy to Food and Drug Administration, Attention: Valerie Potopsingh, Compliance Officer, Human Foods Program – Office of Compliance and Enforcement, Office of Enforcement – Division of Conventional Foods Enforcement (HFS-607), 5001 Campus Drive, College Park, MD 20740. If you have any questions regarding this letter, you may contact Valerie Potopsingh, Compliance Officer, via email at valerie.potopsingh@fda.hhs.gov. Please include reference CMS #730689 on any submissions and within the subject line of any email correspondence to the agency.
